title: Change-Robust Online Topological Memory for Long-Term Relocalization and Semantic Navigation
claim: One sparse memory supports long-horizon navigation and relocalization across lighting, rearrangement, dynamic people and sensor failures, with false matches rejected.
layout: Central 3D map with trajectory; lettered inset callouts (A–G) around it via dotted lines
description: A large textured 3D point-cloud map of an indoor and outdoor loop dominates the figure. A bright green trajectory runs along it, with green and yellow waypoint dots. Dotted lines link these dots to lettered inset panels around the map. (A) shows a language goal, a target location image and a navigation-success image. (B) and (C) pair mapping-session and relocalization-session photos to show appearance change and crowds. (D) shows camera-disconnected (red) and camera-reconnected (green) frames. (E) shows the robot dog among pedestrians. (F1) is a green panel with a small three-step sketch labeled loop closure, accepted. (F2) is a red panel labeled rejected hypothesis, with red crosses. (G) shows a robot dog photo. Green means success and red means failure. The eye goes first to the map and its glowing path.
caption: {CROSS supports long-term semantic navigation with a sparse RGB-D topological memory under lighting variation, object rearrangement, dynamic pedestrians, and sensor degradation. Visual retrievals are lifted into continuous $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ hypotheses, temporally validated by odometry, and only persistent branches are promoted to loop closures or relocalization events.}
abstract: Long-term semantic navigation requires a robot to reuse past observations after appearance and scene change, but semantic memories are only useful if the robot can relocalize into the memory without corrupting it with false visual matches. We propose CROSS, a change-robust topological memory that introduces a pre-commitment localization layer between visual place recognition and map update. Instead of treating a retrieved keyframe as an immediate place association or loop-closure factor, CROSS lifts each RGB-D retrieval into a candidate global SE(3) pose mode using relative pose estimation. A bounded Gaussian-mixture filter then propagates competing continuous trajectory branches with odometry, rejects branches that are physically inconsistent, and promotes only persistent branches to loop closures. This moves ambiguity handling from discrete place IDs or post-hoc graph-factor rejection to continuous pose-space validation before map commitment. Across public long-term relocalization benchmarks and real quadruped object-navigation experiments, CROSS improves reuse of a single sparse RGB-D memory under illumination, seasonal, dynamic-scene, and object-level change. Project page: https://jiaming.im/CROSS/
